entries.claim: With a fresh COPILOT_HOME, does trustedFolders create a blocking first-launch directory-trust gate?
entries.finding: It does, and it is the FIRST gate rather than a secondary one. On a real PTY with a fresh COPILOT_HOME the CLI blocks at launch on a 'Confirm folder trust' dialog with ZERO provider requests, so it precedes the model connection and every tool-approval question. The process stays alive indefinitely: this is the deadlock a detached pane hits. No launch flag clears it -- --allow-all-tools, --allow-all, --yolo, --allow-all-paths and --add-dir <workdir> were each measured still blocking with 0 provider requests. The --yolo row is TCL-1010's and is deliberately not folded into the --allow-all one it duplicates on paper: the CLI documents the two as aliases, and this suite has already been burned once by a documented alias behaving differently -- COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL is documented as the env alias for --allow-all-tools and was measured STRICTLY STRONGER, clearing this very gate (see ambient-allow-all-env). tclaude's `yolo` approval token renders the --yolo spelling and its mode help tells the operator folder trust still blocks, so that spelling is the one that had to be measured. The only measured argv-free bypass is a pre-launch write of {"trustedFolders":["<cwd>"]} into COPILOT_HOME/config.json. A flat trustedFolders key in settings.json was NOT honoured, even though the CLI migrates config.json into settings.json on startup; the nested settings.json spelling, if one exists, is not established here. CONSEQUENCE: Copilot DirTrust is a config-FILE contract, not an argv one, so no ApprovalCatalog argv renderer can produce a launchable detached agent on its own. docs/harnesses.md recording DirTrust=false for Copilot is wrong for interactive launches. Two things for security review rather than silent adoption: the dialog's option 2 is 'Yes, and remember this folder for future sessions', so tclaude writing this key pre-answers a human trust decision; and config.json is JSONC that self-describes as automatically managed, so a naive encoding/json read of an existing file will fail on its comment lines.

entries.claim: Does the default interactive posture block on the first tool call, and does it emit no normal Stop?
entries.finding: It blocks, with one scope limit that must be carried forward. With folder trust already granted and no permission flags, an unsafe shell command ('rm -f ./victim') blocks: the tool result is never posted back, the CLI stays alive with settled output, and the pane shows an approval dialog naming the command. The same command with --allow-all-tools completes -- that positive control is what makes the blocked arm mean something. THE LIMIT: Copilot auto-approves commands it classifies as trivially safe. 'echo ...' executed with no flags at all. So 'blocks on the first tool call' is false as literally stated and true as it matters: it blocks on the first tool call a coding agent would actually make. A matrix built on a safe command alone would have reported the gate as absent. On 'no normal Stop': interactive mode has no JSONL event stream at all (--output-format json is a -p-only surface), and the CLI never exits after a turn -- it sits at its input prompt. So 'process alive with quiet output' does NOT by itself distinguish a blocked launch from a completed idle one, and the tool-result follow-up request is used as the discriminator throughout this suite instead.
corroborating: NOT measured here beyond the two commands this suite samples (echo, rm); reported by the copilot-permission-wire analyst on an independent PTY rig with trust granted and no allow flags: 'echo probe-tool-ran' EXECUTED with no prompt, while 'rm -f victim.txt', 'curl -s https://github.com', 'git push origin main' and 'echo pwned > file.txt' all BLOCKED. Shell redirection counting as a write is the notable one. If it holds, the gate is per-COMMAND risk classification rather than per-tool, which is a materially different thing for a spawner to reason about than a tool allowlist.

NOT measured by anyone, and worth stating so nobody assumes otherwise: the safe-command allowlist is NOT enumerated. Five commands have been sampled across two rigs. A detached-agent default must not be built on a guess about which commands auto-approve; the only safe reading is that ANY command may block unless a permission flag says otherwise.

NOT measured: approval behaviour for the built-in write tools (create/edit). An attempt was made on the peer rig but passed the wrong argument name and returned a schema error, so those rows measure a malformed call rather than an approval outcome. Recorded here specifically so the inconclusive result is not later mistaken for a negative one.

entries.claim: How do URLs behave under --allow-all-tools, and is --deny-tool 'url()' accepted, nonprompting and provider-safe?
entries.finding: DISPROVEN on the flag the TCL-973 plan proposed, and the failure is total: --deny-tool 'url()' is REJECTED at argument parse ('Invalid --deny-tool value. Error: Invalid rule format: url()'), exit 1, provider never contacted. A spawner emitting that default would have killed every Copilot pane at launch. Empty parens are invalid for every kind (shell(), write() likewise) and a bare '*' is invalid, while the bare kind ('url') and kind(pattern) ('url(*)', 'url(example.com)', 'shell(*)', 'write(/tmp)') all parse. Each grammar row asserts two independent signals -- the error text and whether the launch reached the provider -- because an earlier single-signal version of that scenario reported every pattern as accepted, including url(): with COPILOT_OFFLINE=true and no base URL the CLI fails on 'Offline mode requires a local model provider' before it inspects --deny-tool at all. WHAT THIS SUITE MEASURES ABOUT THOSE SPELLINGS IS PARSE ACCEPTANCE ONLY -- whether a pattern is ENFORCED at runtime is a different question no scenario here answers, and for URL rules the two demonstrably come apart (see corroborating). Do not read 'parses' as 'works'. ON THE PROMPT ITSELF, THE MEASUREMENT CORRECTS THE PLAN IN THE PLAN'S OWN FAVOUR, and this row was written expecting the opposite before the real binary said otherwise. With no permission flags, a shell command reaching a URL blocks on a dialog that is unmistakably about the URL ('Copilot is attempting to access the following URL') rather than about the command -- so it IS a distinct prompt with its own chrome and its own decision. But --allow-all-tools CLOSES it: the identical launch with that one flag runs the command through. For the shell path there is therefore no second deadlock to close, and the plan's stated need to pair a URL deny with --allow-all-tools does not follow from this measurement. SCOPE LIMIT, load-bearing: this covers the SHELL path only. Copilot's web-fetch tool is the other URL consumer and is absent from the catalog entirely under COPILOT_OFFLINE=true, which is exactly what makes this suite hermetic -- so whether web_fetch is gated the same way is not something these scenarios can answer, and it is not generalized from the shell result. That gap is now closed by its own entry, web-fetch-url-access, which measures the web-fetch path in a non-offline arm behind a refusing proxy; read the two together. Provider safety is PROVEN CLEAN in the sense this suite can establish, stated precisely because the obvious phrasing overstates it: every URL arm still REACHED the BYOK provider, and the --allow-all-tools arm went on to complete its turn. The no-flags arm did NOT complete -- it blocked at the URL dialog, which is the finding, so it cannot also be cited as evidence of a completed turn. What the pair establishes is that the URL permission layer does not disturb the model connection: the provider is reached either way, and the only thing that stops the turn is the prompt. The whole measurement is hermetic: the gate fires BEFORE any network access is attempted, so nothing is ever dialled.
corroborating: NOT measured by any scenario here; reported by the copilot-permission-wire analyst on an independent rig. Parsing and enforcement come apart for URL rules: 'url(*)', 'url(https://*)', 'url(*.*)', '--deny-url *' and '--deny-url https://*' all parse and then match NOTHING at runtime, falling through to the network layer, whereas domain- and URL-scoped patterns ('url(github.com)', 'url(https://github.com)', 'url(https://*.github.com)', 'url(https://github.com/robots.txt)', '--deny-url github.com') are enforced at the permission layer with no prompt. The two layers are distinguishable by message: 'Permission to access this URL was denied.' versus 'WebFetchBlockedUrlError: ...'.

entries.claim: Does Copilot's web_fetch tool deadlock an unattended pane on a URL prompt, and does the proposed --allow-all-tools --no-ask-user posture close it without reopening egress?
entries.finding: MEASURED, and it closes the gap url-access recorded as structurally unaskable. PRECONDITION: COPILOT_OFFLINE=true removes web_fetch from the advertised catalog entirely, which is why no Phase 0 scenario could ask this. The measurement drops that variable and replaces the hermeticity it provided with an egress wall instead: the BYOK provider stays on loopback via NO_PROXY while proxy-aware non-loopback traffic is routed to a capturing proxy that records a target and answers 502 without dialing it, and the fetched URL is a host under the RFC 2606 reserved .invalid TLD that can never resolve to anything anywhere. Dropping COPILOT_OFFLINE was measured to add web_fetch AND NOTHING ELSE to the catalog, and across the whole matrix the capture proxy recorded no destination other than each run's own probe host -- so the relaxation is the narrow one it is described as, and no auth, telemetry, GitHub MCP or auto-update destination was observed. THAT CONTAINMENT CLAIM IS SCOPED, and the scope is stated rather than glossed: it establishes that all PROXY-AWARE non-loopback traffic went to the refusing capture and that no unexpected destination was observed. It is NOT a kernel-enforced no-egress boundary, and a component ignoring the proxy variables entirely is not ruled out by it. What makes that residual gap acceptable rather than merely acknowledged is that the run carries no credentials (every token variable is scrubbed exactly as in the offline arms), the only model-directed destinations are reserved addresses (RFC 2606 .invalid, RFC 5737 TEST-NET-1) that route nowhere, and no finding here depends on any external access succeeding -- every arm is classified from what the CLI told the model, never from a fetch. The wall is also proven to BE on the path rather than assumed: an 'observed nothing' assertion is satisfied by a CLI that stopped honouring the proxy variables and dialed directly, so a dedicated positive control fetches an unresolvable-but-routable TEST-NET-1 literal and asserts the capture RECORDED it. Without that row every egress assertion in the file would be vacuous. RESULT 1, THE DEADLOCK IS REAL: with folder trust granted and no permission flags, a web_fetch call BLOCKS on the URL dialog ('Copilot is attempting to access the following URL', naming the URL), the tool result is never posted back, the CLI stays alive with settled output, and the capture proxy observed nothing at all. web_fetch is therefore a THIRD independent deadlock source for a detached pane, alongside folder trust and shell tool approval. The conservative posture that kept detached spawn fail-closed while this was unmeasured was correct. RESULT 2, THE PROPOSED POSTURE IS COMPLETE FOR THIS PATH: --allow-all-tools closes it, measured alone so the result cannot be credited to --no-ask-user, and --allow-all-tools --no-ask-user together close it as well. --allow-all-urls alone also closes it, which is what confirms the prompt is a URL decision rather than ordinary tool approval. So url-access's shell-path correction extends to the web-fetch path: the TCL-973 plan's assumption that URL access needs its own grant alongside tool approval holds for NEITHER URL consumer in 1.0.77, and no separate URL flag is required to make an unattended pane nonblocking. RESULT 3, LAYER ORDER, which is what makes the rest of this entry evidence rather than inference: every arm routes proxy-aware traffic to the refusing capture, so 'the fetch did not succeed' is the uninformative default and cannot by itself say anything about the prompt. The three layers are separated by the exact string the CLI posts back to the model -- 'Permission to access this URL was denied.' (permission), "Tool 'web_fetch' does not exist." (absent), and the tool's own 'Failed to fetch <url>' (network). Each is asserted POSITIVELY, which matters most for the allow arms: the classifier reports 'allowed' for any tool result carrying no denial marker, and an absent tool's result qualifies, so an allow arm additionally asserts that the tool ran and reached the transport layer and that its result does NOT say the tool is missing. Otherwise a release that renamed or stopped advertising web_fetch would report this PR's headline conclusion green on a launch where the gate was never reached. The ordering is measured, not assumed, and it is carried by the CONTRAST between rows rather than by any single observation: with an unresolvable host, a deny rule matching it returns the permission-layer string while the same launch without that rule returns 'Failed to fetch'. One row's empty capture would be consistent with either order; the pair is not. So the permission layer runs BEFORE name resolution, and an arm that reached a network error is an arm the permission layer let through. RESULT 4, A WORKING BLANKET URL DENY EXISTS, overturning half of url-access's most consequential corroborating claim: the BARE KIND '--deny-tool url', with no parentheses, denies every URL at the permission layer with no prompt and no name resolution, and it does so while paired with --allow-all-tools --no-ask-user -- so a LAUNCH-TIME deny beats a LAUNCH-TIME blanket allow on the URL axis, exactly as in-pane-allow-all-override established for the shell axis. Stated at that width deliberately: whether the deny also survives POST-LAUNCH widening from inside the pane is not measured here, so nothing may call it a durable boundary on this entry's evidence. The wildcard half of that claim is confirmed: 'url(*)', '--deny-url *' and '--deny-url https://*' all parse and then match NOTHING, falling through to the network layer. Host-scoped 'url(<host>)' and '--deny-url <host>' are enforced. PARSE ACCEPTANCE IS STILL NOT ENFORCEMENT; the difference here is that enforcement is now measured per spelling rather than inferred from any of them. RESULT 5, REMOVAL AS AN ALTERNATIVE TO GRANTING: '--excluded-tools web_fetch' removes the tool from the catalog and nothing else, and the exact identifier is 'web_fetch' -- proven rather than guessed, since a spawner excluding 'webfetch' or 'web-fetch' would exclude nothing while reading as if it had. A model that calls the excluded tool anyway does NOT deadlock: the CLI answers "Tool 'web_fetch' does not exist", lists the tools that do, and the turn continues, with no permission flag granted anywhere in the launch and no network reached. This is the option a fail-closed detached posture wants, because it removes the capability instead of permitting it. It does NOT cover URL access performed through the shell tool (curl/wget in bash), which is a separate path url-access measures. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE APPROVAL-CORE ARGV: --allow-all-tools --no-ask-user is nonblocking for web_fetch, so web_fetch is no longer a reason to keep detached spawn fail-closed. A launch that additionally wants no outbound web tool should add '--excluded-tools web_fetch' (capability removal) or '--deny-tool url' (blanket permission-layer deny); both are nonblocking, and neither is required merely to avoid a deadlock.
corroborating: NOT measured here: whether web_fetch prompts differently for a host that RESOLVES. Every arm here targets a reserved .invalid host (the egress-wall control targets RFC 5737 TEST-NET-1 instead -- also reserved, a different reservation), which is what keeps the run contained. The permission layer was measured to run before name resolution, so a resolvable host cannot reach the gate any differently -- but the ALLOWED arms would proceed further into the network layer than these did, and nothing here observes that.

NOT measured: whether the bare-kind '--deny-tool url' survives post-launch widening from inside the pane (/allow-all, or a persisted allowedUrls entry). This entry establishes launch-time precedence only. It must be fixtured before any tclaude tool-governance surface renders a URL deny, because a blanket deny a pane can widen away is a different product from one it cannot.

NOT measured here: the post-authentication destination set. This arm is credential-free, so the CLI never completes a token exchange, and a launch that did might reach hosts no run here can observe. The proxy establishes what an unauthenticated online-arm launch dials, which is what the hermeticity claim needs, and not more.

NOT measured here, and it is the boundary of the containment mechanism rather than of the behavioural finding: the destination set is proxy-observed, not kernel-observed. A component that ignored HTTP(S)_PROXY/ALL_PROXY entirely would not appear in the capture. A process-level network namespace would close this, but it would also cut the loopback route to the mock provider that every scenario depends on, and it does not exist on both supported platforms; the reserved-address targets and the credential-free environment are what the arm relies on instead.

entries.claim: How does an ambient COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL promote a launch, so a spawner can scrub or override it?
entries.finding: It promotes silently and it is STRICTLY STRONGER THAN THE FLAG IT DOCUMENTS. --help presents COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL as the env alias for --allow-all-tools, but the flag does not clear the folder-trust gate and the variable does: with no flags whatsoever and only COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL=true in the environment, a fresh-COPILOT_HOME launch skipped the trust dialog, reached the provider and executed an unsafe tool call. Parsing is strict, case-sensitive equality against the literal string 'true' -- 'TRUE', '1', 'false' and '' all behave exactly as unset. CONSEQUENCE: an operator with this exported turns every tclaude-spawned Copilot pane into an allow-all session with no record anywhere, so EnvExports must UNSET it rather than pin it to a falsy value. Unsetting is the only treatment that cannot be defeated by a future widening of the value parse.

It does. Measured on the advertised tool catalog in the provider request body, which is the strongest instrument in this matrix because it is a pure wire read that depends on neither TUI scraping nor the model choosing to call anything. On a PTY with trust granted the default catalog offers ask_user; adding --no-ask-user removes it and nothing else. This closes the second independent deadlock source, since ask_user is how the model stops to ask a question nobody is present to answer. It requires a PTY to measure: ask_user is only advertised when there is a terminal to ask through, so headless the flag is a no-op and a headless scenario would report it working while measuring nothing.

entries.claim: What is the out-of-cwd/temp access behavior, and what exactly do --add-dir and --disallow-temp-dir do?
entries.finding: PLATFORM SCOPE: this is the one measurement in the matrix required on BOTH supported platforms, because its subject IS platform semantics -- the cwd-subtree and system-temp grants and which spellings of them the CLI honours. Everything else here measures prompt behaviour that lives in the CLI's own JavaScript. A finding about Linux temp semantics is not a finding about macOS temp semantics, and macOS resolves TMPDIR through a /var -> /private/var symlink that Linux does not have. Paths are a SEPARATE deadlock source with their own dialog, 'Allow directory access', distinct from both folder trust (which gates the whole launch) and tool approval (which gates the command). Measured on a PTY with trust pre-granted: a shell read of a path outside every granted root BLOCKS on that dialog, which names the offending path and offers to add it to the allowed list. --add-dir <dir> and --allow-all-paths each clear it. The system temp dir is granted automatically, and --disallow-temp-dir removes that grant, after which a read inside temp blocks the same way. Both flags therefore work as named. The scenario carries an exact internal control: the identical 'cat' command is ALLOWED inside the granted temp dir and BLOCKED outside it, so the block is demonstrably path-driven rather than command-risk-driven. CORRECTION TO A HEADLESS RESULT, and it is the third time in this ticket that a no-TTY measurement pointed the wrong way: measured headlessly, an out-of-grant path AUTO-DENIES -- the CLI answers the model 'Permission denied and could not request permission from user' and the turn continues. From there paths look like the one prompt surface a detached agent need not worry about, because it resolves itself. On a real terminal the same launch stops and waits forever. Note this is the OPPOSITE asymmetry from tool approval, whose no-TTY fallback auto-ALLOWS: two different fallbacks in the same binary, neither of which describes a pane. SAFETY: --allow-all-paths is measured here only to characterize the mechanism and must never be a default. Copilot's built-in edits are not OS-confined (TCL-977), so the path check is the only file-write boundary a launch outside tclaude-layer has.
corroborating: NOT measured here: whether the directory-access dialog's option 2 ('add these directories to the allowed list') persists the grant to disk the way the folder-trust dialog's option 2 does. If it does, that is a third persistence surface alongside trustedFolders and allowedUrls, and a spawner would need to reason about it.

entries.finding: It does. With folder trust pre-granted on a real PTY, the out-of-grant shell read in TestCopilotPermissionPathGrants/outside-all/allow-all-tools was launched with --allow-all-tools as its only permission flag and still produced PermissionBlocked: exactly one provider request, no tool-result follow-up, a live process with settled output, and the positive 'Allow directory access' dialog naming the target path. Before TCL-992, the five existing TestCopilotPermissionPathGrants rows inherited RunPTY's default --allow-all-tools, so out-of-cwd-paths already measured this posture without naming it. TCL-992 sets OmitAllowAllTools for the full six-row matrix, making those five rows the newly isolated no-flag/path postures while this explicit row preserves the historical allow-all-tools measurement; the complete six-row matrix was rerun green against pinned 1.0.77. CONSEQUENCE: the load-bearing --add-dir design and the refusal of a deny nested inside a grant remain valid outside tclaude-layer; tool approval does not erase Copilot's own directory boundary.

entries.claim: Does --add-dir grant writes as well as reads?
entries.finding: It does. With folder trust pre-granted and tool approval closed explicitly by --allow-all-tools, the positive PTY row ran 'echo ... > <outside>/copilotfixture-write-probe.txt' under --add-dir <outside>, returned PermissionAllowed, and read back the exact committed probe content. The sibling with the same write command, trust, and tool flag but no --add-dir was PermissionBlocked on the positive 'Allow directory access' dialog, naming the target, with exactly one provider request and no created file. This isolates the write grant from tool approval and proves that Copilot's single directory-access grant covers both read and write operations.

entries.claim: Does Copilot 1.0.77 accept an abbreviated, camelCase, or --no- spelling of an audited option?
entries.finding: It does not. Each spelling was launched on a real PTY with folder trust pre-granted and a credential-free mock provider: --allow-all-tool (prefix abbreviation), --allowAllTools (camelCase), and --no-allow-all-tools (negation) all exited 1 with an 'unknown option' diagnostic and zero provider requests. The parser probe therefore establishes that ValidateLaunchExtraArgs' exact flag-name matching is sound for these bypass shapes; the audit still separately handles the documented =value and glued single-dash forms.

entries.claim: Does -i combined with --resume=<full-id> submit the prompt into the resumed conversation?
entries.finding: It does. Two-phase, both against the real binary: phase one seeds a conversation under a pinned --session-id, phase two relaunches it on a PTY with --resume=<full-id> and a new -i prompt. The resumed request carried message roles [system, user, assistant, user] -- the earlier exchange followed by the new turn -- and the session-state directory stayed under the original UUID, so the conversation kept its identity rather than forking. A fresh conversation would have sent [system, user], which is what makes this instrument exact rather than suggestive. This retires the standing UNVERIFIED comment in copilot_spawner.go and means relaunch briefings do not vanish silently.
corroborating: NOT measured, and it is where the real risk lives: --resume also accepts id PREFIXES and session NAMES (exact, case-insensitive). Only the full-UUID form is established here. A non-full id or a name collision would attach a relaunch to a different conversation entirely, which argues for a UUID-shape guard at the spawn boundary rather than for relaxing one.

entries.claim: Can in-pane /allow-all override a launch-time --deny-tool, i.e. are launch permission flags a durable boundary or only startup posture?
entries.finding: DISPROVEN, and this is the favourable direction: in-pane /allow-all CANNOT override a launch-time deny. Measured on a PTY with a session launched under --deny-tool 'shell(echo)'. The pane accepted the widening command and confirmed 'All permissions are now enabled' -- asserted, so the scenario cannot pass by failing to deliver it -- and the tool requested afterwards was still refused, with 'Permission to run this tool was denied' posted back as the tool result. Denial precedence therefore holds at RUNTIME, not merely at launch. The command choice is load-bearing: 'echo' is auto-approved when no rule mentions it, so the refusal can only come from the deny rule and no risk-classification confound can explain it away. CONSEQUENCE: a launch-time --deny-tool is a real boundary rather than a starting posture, so TCL-973 plan risk 5 can be softened for denies specifically.
corroborating: NOT measured: the other in-pane mutators (/add-dir, /reset-allowed-tools, /settings, /experimental), and whether the ALLOW posture rather than a deny can be widened in-pane. A durable deny says nothing about those, and neither docs nor a spawner should generalize from one to the other. The URL axis is likewise unmeasured for in-pane widening; see web-fetch-url-access.

NOT measured: whether a deny also survives the ambient COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL=true promotion, which clears gates no flag can. Denial precedence beating an in-pane command does not establish it beating the environment variable.

entries.claim: What does the --yolo flag actually close, and what does it leave standing? tclaude's `yolo` approval token renders it, so the answer decides what that token's mode help may claim.
entries.finding: MEASURED, on all three axes the token speaks about, each with its own PTY row and each against the --yolo SPELLING rather than the --allow-all alias the CLI documents beside it. RESULT 1, TOOL APPROVAL CLOSES: the unsafe shell command ('rm -f ./victim') that BLOCKS with no permission flags at all ran to completion under --yolo alone, with the tool result posted back to the provider (TestCopilotPermissionToolApprovalGate/unsafe-command/yolo). The command choice is load-bearing and is the same one default-interactive-blocking established: Copilot auto-approves what it classifies as trivially safe, so only an unsafe command can distinguish a CLOSED gate from an ABSENT one, and the no-flags sibling in that same table is the negative control that makes the allowed verdict mean something. RESULT 2, THE DIRECTORY DIALOG CLOSES, which is the axis the token exists for: the identical out-of-grant 'cat' that PermissionBlocked under --allow-all-tools (path-dialog-under-allow-all-tools) returned PermissionAllowed under --yolo (TestCopilotPermissionPathGrants/outside-all/yolo). The two rows are the same command, the same staged out-of-every-grant directory and the same pinned TMPDIR, differing only in the flag, so this is a CONTRAST between two launches rather than a claim about one. --add-dir remains necessary under the unattended `allow-tools` default; it is merely redundant under this token. RESULT 3, FOLDER TRUST DOES NOT CLOSE, and this is the honesty limit the mode help must carry: with a fresh COPILOT_HOME, --yolo blocked at the folder-trust dialog with ZERO provider requests, exactly as every other flag does (TestCopilotPermissionTrustBypassSurface/yolo, and see folder-trust). No approval token can make a fresh-COPILOT_HOME launch complete on its own; trust stays a config-FILE contract handled by tclaude's trust_dir path. NOT MEASURED, and therefore not claimed anywhere: whether --yolo also removes the ask_user tool. The catalog renders --no-ask-user alongside it rather than assuming, because that axis has its own measurement (no-ask-user) and it is the advertised tool CATALOG that changes there, not an approval. Likewise unmeasured is whether --allow-all behaves identically; the alias claim is the CLI's, not this suite's, and nothing tclaude renders depends on it. CONSEQUENCE: a `yolo` token is renderable honestly -- but the evidence that it works was never the argument for it. Copilot's built-in file edits are not OS-confined (TCL-977), so outside --sandbox-impl tclaude-layer the directory check RESULT 2 removes is the only file boundary the launch has, which is why the token ships with a spawn-time warning on the un-sandboxed pairing rather than with mode-help copy alone.

entries.claim: Does Copilot 1.0.77 expose a per-launch flag that selects its own command-sandbox posture, as tclaude's contract says it does not?
entries.finding: IT DOES, and the standing 'there is no launch flag' premise in harness/copilot_sandbox.go and docs/harnesses.md is wrong for 1.0.77 -- but the flag is unusable for the posture tclaude would want, for a reason the flag's existence alone does not reveal. `--sandbox` and `--no-sandbox` were added in 1.0.70 ('turn the OS-level shell sandbox on or off for the current session only, without changing your saved sandbox setting'), are ABSENT from `copilot --help` on 1.0.77 (asserted, not merely observed -- anchored on the option-row spelling, since the help text also lists `sandbox` as a help TOPIC), and are accepted by the parser -- proven against an impossible neighbour spelling that is rejected with 'unknown option', so acceptance is not a parser that swallows anything. THE GATE: without `--experimental` both flags are parsed and then IGNORED, in both directions -- a `--no-sandbox` launch against `sandbox.enabled: true` is still enforced, and a `--sandbox` launch against `enabled: false` is still unconfined. WITH `--experimental` both are honoured and override the settings file in both directions. `--experimental` ALONE changes nothing, which is the control that stops the honoured rows being credited to it. CONSEQUENCE, and it is the whole answer for a copilot-native posture: the only argv that selects the sandbox is the same argv that registers the in-pane `/sandbox enable|disable` command, which CopilotTclaudeLayerExtraArgRefusal refuses and ValidateCopilotTclaudeLayerInnerSandbox refuses over precisely because a pane can then revoke the posture mid-session. A per-launch override available only together with an in-pane override of itself is not a recorded, durable posture. SECOND PROPERTY, measured because it would be the dangerous one: neither flag PERSISTS. After a `--sandbox --experimental` run against `enabled: false`, ResolveCopilotInnerSandbox still reports false, and likewise for `--no-sandbox` over `enabled: true` -- so the flags do not silently edit the operator's configuration. The instrument throughout is a built-in `create` into a deniedPaths entry rather than a shell command, which is what makes every row valid on a host whose OS backend cannot start.
corroborating: NOT measured: whether an in-pane `/sandbox disable` under `--sandbox --experimental` really does revoke the launch-selected posture mid-session. The refusal contract assumes it can, and the command's registration is documented; the runtime effect on an already-running turn needs a PTY scenario. Nothing here should be read as having proven the revocation, only the registration.

NOT measured: whether `/settings set` can write the `sandbox` key from inside a pane WITHOUT experimental features, which would be a second in-pane mutation path the experimental gate does not cover. `copilot help config` does not list `sandbox` among its keys at all, so the key's status in the settings UI is unestablished.

NOT measured, and taken from the bundled changelog.json rather than from behaviour: that the flags were ADDED in 1.0.70. Only their presence and gating on 1.0.77 are measured here; the version they arrived in is provenance, not a finding.

entries.claim: What does the OS policy Copilot's MXC backend generates on Linux actually contain?
entries.finding: CAPTURED, by shimming `bwrap` first on PATH and recording the argument vector; on Linux that argv IS the policy, since bubblewrap has no configuration file. The measurement works on BOTH host categories the suite distinguishes, because the policy is generated before the namespace is attempted -- so it is the one sandbox scenario that needs no usable backend. SHAPE (1.0.77): `--unshare-user --unshare-pid --unshare-ipc --unshare-uts`, then `--ro-bind-try` of the system trees (/bin /sbin /lib* /usr/{bin,sbin,lib*,libexec,share} /etc) and of the resolver runtime dirs, `--symlink /run /var/run`, `--dev /dev`, `--proc /proc`, `--tmpfs /tmp` plus a `--bind` of TMPDIR, a `--ro-bind` for EVERY directory on the launching process's PATH, a read-write `--bind` of the workspace, `--chdir` into it, `--clearenv`, one `--setenv` per inherited variable, and finally `-- sh -c "/bin/bash --norc --noprofile -c '<command>'"`. The argument COUNT is deliberately not recorded: it is a property of the measuring machine's PATH and environment size, not of the release. FOUR FINDINGS THE OUTSIDE-IN SCENARIOS CANNOT SEE. (1) NETWORK IS THE ONE DIMENSION THAT IS KERNEL-ENFORCED END TO END: `--unshare-net` is present exactly when `network.allowOutbound` is false and absent when it is true, measured in both directions. An unshared network namespace with no interfaces cannot be talked around, unlike the filesystem half whose built-in-edit path never enters the sandbox at all. (2) A deniedPaths ENTRY IS NOT A DENY RULE -- it is `--tmpfs <path>`, an empty filesystem mounted over the target. That is MASKING rather than denial, and the two are indistinguishable from outside: every existing scenario asserts only that the host file is absent, which both satisfy equally, so nothing before this entry could tell them apart. What a masked write looks like to the MODEL is a separate question no scenario here answers; see corroborating. (3) `--clearenv` READS LIKE A SCRUB AND IS NOT ONE, and the ASYMMETRY is the finding rather than the inheritance. A planted GITHUB_TOKEN arrives inside the sandbox verbatim while a planted OPENAI_API_KEY is DROPPED -- so the fixed blocklist `copilot help sandbox` mentions is real and is doing work, and it does not cover the credential most likely to be live in a shell that launches Copilot. Both rows are asserted, and the dropped one is the control: without it, the inherited row would be consistent with no filtering at all. Copilot's sandbox is a filesystem and network boundary, not a credential one. (4) THE READ-ONLY BIND SET FOLLOWS THE LAUNCHING PROCESS'S PATH, which matters to tclaude specifically: whatever PATH it hands a Copilot pane decides part of the sandbox's executable surface. Asserted rather than observed -- the scenario puts its own shim directory on PATH and the generated policy `--ro-bind`s it.
corroborating: NOT measured, and deliberately so: the macOS Seatbelt profile. The darwin backend goes through `sandbox-exec` with a generated profile rather than a bubblewrap argv, so capturing it needs a different shim and a different reader; writing that reader on a machine that cannot run it would put an unmeasured assertion into CI. Every policy-content claim in this entry is Linux-only, and the scenario skips on other platforms rather than pretending otherwise.

NOT measured: what a write into a masked (deniedPaths) directory looks like from INSIDE a live namespace, and therefore what the model is told. `--tmpfs` semantics imply the write succeeds into a throwaway filesystem rather than failing, which would mean the model can be told a denied write succeeded -- but that is a reading of bubblewrap, not an observation, and this scenario never starts a namespace. It is measurable on a host whose backend runs, by asserting on the shell tool RESULT for a denied path rather than only on host-file absence, and that is the natural next scenario.

NOT measured: whether `--unshare-net` is the whole network story. `network.allowLocalNetwork` was true in both arms, and 1.0.60's changelog mentions allowedHosts/blockedHosts handling, so a host-list posture may generate more than the namespace switch this matrix crosses.

NOT measured as an assertion, only observed in the recorded argv: no `--die-with-parent`, no `--new-session`, and no seccomp filter appear in the generated policy. Recorded because their absence is a real property of the boundary, but nothing pins it, since a future release adding any of them would be a tightening rather than a regression.

entries.claim: What does `sandbox.allowBypass` do, and does autopilot disable the sandbox as the 1.0.77 changelog says?
entries.finding: `allowBypass` CHANGES THE KIND OF BOUNDARY. With the key true, a policy violation stops being a refusal and becomes a PERMISSION REQUEST -- the tool result changes from the sandbox's own 'sandbox is active and blocked ...' to the CLI's ordinary 'Permission denied and could not request permission from user', which is what an unanswerable prompt produces. So a Copilot sandbox with allowBypass on is not a boundary but a question, and the answer decides the boundary. Every arm still failed closed -- the file never reached the host -- which is exactly why this is a finding about MECHANISM that no landed-or-not assertion could have produced. WHAT THE MATRIX ESTABLISHES ABOUT AUTOPILOT IS NARROW, and is stated narrowly because the investigation reached this key from a 1.0.77 changelog entry -- 'Unconditional autopilot approval now disables sandbox for the current session when bypass is allowed' -- that it does NOT refute. Crossed with `--autopilot` and `--yolo`, neither flag changes the outcome at launch in either direction: `allowBypass` alone decides it. That is a fact about LAUNCH FLAGS, not about the changelog's subject, which is an in-pane approval decision this headless matrix never reaches. The two results are consistent; nothing here contradicts the vendor. NOTE ON THE SCHEMA: `allowBypass` is documented by `copilot help sandbox` and named in the shipped runtime, but is NOT a property of SandboxConfig in schemas/api.schema.json, which declares additionalProperties:false. The matrix measures what the key does rather than trusting either source.
corroborating: NOT measured, and it is the half that decides how bad this is: whether the bypass prompt AUTO-APPROVES on a real terminal. These runs carry the runner's default --allow-all-tools and it did not approve the bypass, but the permission matrix's out-of-cwd-paths entry establishes that a no-TTY launch takes DIFFERENT fallbacks from a pane (auto-deny for paths, auto-allow for tools), so a headless denial says nothing about a pane.

NOT measured: the changelog's actual claim -- that an unconditional autopilot APPROVAL disables the sandbox for the rest of the session. That path runs through an in-pane approval decision, so it needs a PTY scenario; the launch-flag rows here cannot reach it and must not be read as having tested it.
NOT measured: whether the bypass prompt, once approved, drops the sandbox for the single command or for the rest of the session.
